To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the tendency to compare oneself to others in terms of income does not moderate the negative effect of inequality on health, nor the health differences that exist between those at the top and the bottom of the income distribution.

The propensity of people to make social comparisons does not contribute to explaining the negative effect of high income inequality on health, nor the health differences between those with higher and lower relative incomes.

(1) social comparison orientation does not explain the negative effect of relative income on health; (2) social comparison orientation is not associated with self-rated overall health; and (3) social comparison orientation explains a small part of the variation in psychological well-being.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social mechanisms that explain why social determinants of population health matter.
a key mechanism of the relationship between social stratification, social comparisons, and health.
the question of how income differences between people are related to their health and well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
social comparison orientation is not a relevant mechanism explaining socio-economic disparities and income inequality in health.
social comparison processes do not seem to play a significant role in the income inequality-health relationship.
social comparisons play no role in explaining the health differences between countries and within countries by income inequality or by income position.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the tendency to engage in social comparison is an important factor in the relationship between income and health, but that the role of social comparisons as a link between income inequality and health is less clear.
the mechanism of social comparisons does not seem to play a significant role in explaining the income gradient or the income inequality-health relationship.
income inequality does not seem to have a direct effect on health, nor does the socio-economic gradient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social comparison processes do not appear to contribute to the explanation of socio-economic differences in health.
the mechanism of social comparison orientation is not an important determinant of the income inequality-health relationship.
the social gradient in health and income inequality are not explained by the tendency to compare oneself to others.
